name: Subjects
tagline: A South African education tool built around school subjects, study material and learner progress.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software layer here is not the hard part: subjects, topics, progress bars, a study planner and a quiz loop are all standard CRUD plus a scheduling algorithm, and an agent will produce a working local version quickly. What you cannot generate is the curriculum-aligned content: notes, past papers, memos, worked solutions and anything mapped to a specific national syllabus. If the value you get from this is mostly organising your own material, build it. If the value is that someone already did the syllabus mapping and keeps it current every year, you are paying for a content library with an app bolted on, and that does not one-shot. Verdict sits at kinda because the split depends entirely on which half you actually use.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you define subjects and topics, attach your own notes and past papers, log study sessions, and get a spaced repetition queue of self-written questions.
requirements: Node 20 and a local machine to run it on
Your own notes, textbooks or past papers to load in
Willingness to type your own flashcards instead of getting them prewritten
whatYouLose: Curriculum-aligned content: notes, past papers, memos and worked solutions you did not write
Content that gets updated when the syllabus or exam format changes
Any teacher, school or parent view of progress
A mobile app that works on a cheap phone with patchy data
Marking or feedback on anything longer than a multiple choice answer
moatNotes: Education products in a single country live or die on syllabus fidelity. That is a licensing and editorial job, not a coding one.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because nobody wants to author a year of curriculum content to save a subscription, and a learner three weeks from finals is buying material and structure, not software. There is also a trust element: parents and schools pay for something that visibly matches the official syllabus and gets refreshed each year, and a homemade tracker cannot claim that. The app is the delivery mechanism; the content is the product.
notes: Build it if you already have the material and just want it organised. Buy it if you are paying for the syllabus mapping.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user study tracker web app called "Study Desk". No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript and Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/study.db, created and migrated on first run
- Server actions for all writes, no separate API layer
- Runs with `npm install && npm run dev` on http://localhost:3000

Data model:
- Subject: name, grade or level, colour, exam date (optional)
- Topic: belongs to a Subject, name, weight, confidence rating 1 to 5, notes as markdown
- Resource: belongs to a Topic or Subject, title, type (note, past paper, memo, link, file path), url or local path
- StudySession: subject, topic, minutes, date, freeform log
- Card: belongs to a Topic, question, answer, SM-2 fields (ease, interval, due date, reps)

Features in scope:
- Subject dashboard: topics listed by confidence, days until exam, total minutes logged
- Topic page: markdown notes editor, resource list, cards list
- Review mode: pull cards due today across all subjects, show question, reveal answer, grade 1 to 4, apply SM-2 scheduling
- Study timer: pick subject and topic, start/stop, writes a StudySession
- Weekly plan page: suggests time per subject weighted by exam proximity, topic weight and low confidence, as a plain table
- Markdown import: drop .md files into ./import and a button that turns each file into a Topic with notes
- JSON export of the whole database from a settings page

Explicitly out of scope: no prewritten curriculum content, no AI question generation, no auth, no multi-user, no mobile app, no PDF parsing, no marking of long answers. Seed the database with two example subjects and six cards so the review loop is testable immediately.

Write a README that states plainly: this organises material you supply, it does not supply material.
